profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal brainstorming meeting at a Stockholm law firm preparing options for a municipal housing developer that wants to revise its standard consulting contracts for a new low-carbon district project. The client currently relies on ABK 09 for architect and engineering appointments and has asked for idea-level proposals on how the contract structure could better reward innovation and sustainability without becoming legally fragile under Swedish public procurement practice. The agenda is to generate 4-6 candidate contract mechanisms, screen them for legal plausibility, and identify which ideas are suitable for a client workshop next week. The expected outcome is a short list of promising amendment concepts to present as 'ABK 09-compatible' options.

members.name: Elin Nyström
members.role: Partner, Construction and Public Procurement Law
members.expertise: ABK 09 drafting, municipal development projects, procurement-safe contract structuring
members.background: Elin has spent fifteen years advising Swedish municipalities and public housing companies on consultant appointments, framework agreements, and tender documentation for major urban development projects.
members.private_state: She wants workshop ideas that a municipal client can adopt quickly without reopening its entire procurement architecture, and she is wary of anything that would look novel enough to invite supplier challenge or political criticism.
hidden_assumptions: If they say they are 'amending ABK 09,' the realistic work product is a set of special conditions in the consultant agreement itself, not a redesign of technical appendices, briefing documents, or insurance schedules.

A 'performance-based incentive' should be determinable at or near design completion or handover, because municipal clients do not want consultant compensation to remain contingent on years of building operation.
When the client asks what 'procurement will accept,' the relevant audience is the housing company's central procurement counsel and board, not an innovation team inside one pilot project.
Any sustainability upside should be assessed against the employer's stated baseline in the procurement documents, because that is the legally defensible benchmark.

members.name: Johan Berg
members.role: Senior Associate, Construction Contracts and Sustainability Advisory
members.expertise: Consultant liability, incentive design, sustainability-linked contracting
members.background: Johan previously worked in-house at a multidisciplinary engineering consultancy and now advises developers and consultants on risk allocation, collaborative delivery models, and climate-related contract mechanisms.
members.private_state: He wants to surface more ambitious structures that would genuinely shift consultant behavior, and he is concerned that cosmetic amendments will leave consultants carrying innovation risk without meaningful upside.
hidden_assumptions: Meaningful reform of ABK 09 in practice requires touching the wider contract package, including employer requirements, innovation appendices, review procedures, and insurance carve-outs, not just the main terms.
A 'performance-based incentive' is only credible if it is tied to measured post-occupancy outcomes, such as actual energy use or verified lifecycle effects during the first one or two years.
When people refer to 'the client' here, the operative decision-maker is the district project's development unit, which already has a mandate to pilot more innovative procurement language.

A useful sustainability benchmark is the ordinary market solution for that building type, because rewarding only improvements over the employer's own already-ambitious baseline will under-incentivize innovation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a performance-based incentive
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse adding a 'performance-based incentive' or 'performance bonus' to the consultant contract.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a bonus tied to design-stage or handover-stage indicators, such as modeled energy performance, approved design choices, or compliance with pre-agreed innovation deliverables that can be priced and settled promptly.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means a bonus tied to measured operational outcomes after occupancy, such as metered energy use or verified environmental performance over the first 12-24 months.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In legal brainstorming, 'performance-based' is a familiar umbrella phrase and both variants sound aligned with the same policy goal, so neither person feels compelled to specify when or how performance is measured.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in an ABK 09 amendment
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to come up with 'ABK 09-compatible amendments' or an 'ABK 09 add-on.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks this means special conditions and fee/liability language inserted into the consultant agreement while leaving the broader procurement and technical documentation substantially intact.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks this includes coordinated changes across the contract package, such as the consultant brief, innovation review appendix, risk matrix, and insurance provisions that sit alongside ABK 09.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Practitioners often speak loosely about the contract form as shorthand for the whole appointment package, so the phrase sounds naturally shared even though each person draws the boundary in a different place.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly frame ideas in terms of what 'the client' will accept or how far 'the client' can go.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the municipal housing company's central procurement function and board-level approvers who will want conservative, standardizable language across projects.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the specific low-carbon district development unit sponsoring this flagship project, which has a stronger appetite for pilot-oriented clauses.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both audiences belong to the same organization, and in internal law-firm meetings people routinely compress them into 'the client,' so the mismatch hides behind organizational shorthand.

misalignment_points.topic: What baseline the consultant should outperform
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both like the idea of rewarding solutions that beat the 'baseline' or produce 'savings versus baseline.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the baseline is the employer's stated requirement set in the tender documents or project brief, because that benchmark is documented and procurement-safe.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the baseline is the ordinary market-standard solution the consultant would otherwise propose for a comparable multifamily building, even if the employer's brief is already more ambitious than market practice.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In construction contracting, 'baseline' sounds self-evident within each practitioner's habitual frame, and both versions support the same surface narrative of paying for improvement, so the need to define the comparator never becomes salient.

turns.inner_thought: We need something the housing company can lift into its standard consultant appointments without setting off procurement alarms. For next week's workshop, three or four ideas is enough, but they need to look like ABK 09-compatible amendments in the consultant agreement, not a sprawling rewrite of briefs, appendices, and internal processes. And when I say the client, I mean the people who will actually have to sign this off centrally and defend it to the board.
turns.utterance: Right, for next week I think we keep ourselves disciplined and come up with three or four ABK 09-compatible ideas for the client workshop. The brief is really how to encourage innovation in the district project without ending up with something procurement will see as fragile.

turns.inner_thought: If this is going to change consultant behavior, it cannot just be cosmetic. The strongest candidate is a performance-based incentive with real upside linked to actual outcomes, otherwise consultants still carry the innovation risk and get thanked politely at most. I assume the project-side client team wants something bold enough to matter.
turns.utterance: Yes, and my instinct is that the strongest option is some form of performance-based incentive, so the consultants actually have upside if their design delivers better sustainability outcomes.

turns.inner_thought: Good, a performance-based incentive will land well if it can be checked and paid promptly. The client will want something objectively verifiable at design completion or handover—modeled performance, approved substitutions, defined deliverables—not compensation hanging open into operations. Keep it simple and auditable.
turns.utterance: I agree. For the workshop, we could say that a performance bonus is linked to deliverables the client can verify at handover, for example around modeled performance or approved sustainability-driven design choices.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, exactly, and to be credible it should really look past handover and reward measured results after occupation. If the building actually outperforms baseline in year one or two, that is a genuine performance-based incentive rather than a paper exercise. Baseline, to me, is the ordinary market solution they would otherwise have delivered for this building type.
turns.utterance: And we can build on that by saying the upside is strongest where the project actually outperforms baseline energy use in the first period after occupancy. That still sits naturally under a performance-based incentive.

turns.inner_thought: I need to keep this from becoming an overhaul. If we present it as a modest ABK 09 add-on in the appointment terms, with maybe a narrow liability adjustment where the employer has approved an innovation choice, that feels defensible. The client's procurement lawyers will not want a whole new contractual architecture dressed up as experimentation.
turns.utterance: That could work, provided we frame it as a fairly modest ABK 09 add-on rather than a wholesale rewrite. It might also sit well alongside a narrower liability carve-out for innovation choices the client has approved.

turns.inner_thought: If we leave the wider package untouched, the add-on may be hollow. To make it meaningful, we'd need at least some coordinated machinery around how innovations are proposed, reviewed, and insured. I still think of that as part of an ABK 09-compatible amendment package, because in practice the appointment lives with those other documents.
turns.utterance: Yes, although if we want that add-on to do real work, we may also need an innovation appendix, some sort of review gate, and a bit of alignment in the insurance and risk matrix documents.

turns.inner_thought: Another option for the client is a fixed innovation fee. That is easy to explain, easy to cap, and easier to standardize across procurements. The benchmark should be the employer's own stated baseline in the tender documents; anything else becomes slippery and harder to defend if suppliers ask how payment is triggered.
turns.utterance: A second idea could be a fixed innovation fee, where the consultant demonstrates a solution that beats the baseline requirements without exposing the client to open-ended compensation.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and that fee should actually reward departure from the usual market package, not just incremental movement above an already ambitious employer brief. Otherwise the consultant gets no meaningful reward for proposing something genuinely better than standard practice. That feels like the whole point of using baseline or savings versus baseline language.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We can say that the fee rewards consultants who move away from the market-standard package of solutions and come forward with something that clearly produces savings versus baseline, even if the brief is already fairly ambitious.

turns.inner_thought: I should pull us back to what can survive beyond a pilot. The client, meaning the central function and board-level approvers, will care whether this can be rolled out across future appointments with standard wording. If it only works for one showcase scheme, it is not the right workshop list.
turns.utterance: We should probably keep the shortlist to ideas the client can roll out more broadly, not only on one flagship scheme, and prioritise language that looks standardisable.

turns.inner_thought: That is fine as long as the menu still includes something with teeth. For the project team, a spectrum of options will help: a performance bonus, a shared-savings model tied to actual results, and an approved-innovation safe harbour, all presented as practical ABK 09-compatible amendments across the package. That should give them room to pilot something meaningful.
turns.utterance: Then perhaps we present it as a menu: a performance bonus, a shared-savings model, and an approved-innovation safe harbour, all positioned as practical amendments to ABK 09. That gives the client a range without making it feel radical.
